segment:
Jonah had very warm palms; there was calloused skin on his right one, around the fingers but not the thumb. He didn’t look nervous, but his grip was firm and his smile seemed a little brittle, as though he were trying to keep hold of something.
Then his grip loosened. “Um—” His eyes flickered past Mara toward the open door. A low voice was speaking out in the hall—a man’s voice, saying something she couldn’t quite catch, and another voice replying in a woman’s light tone. She heard a small click and knew they would be in the room any moment now.

“I’m Mara,” she said into the silence.
“Mara,” Jonah repeated, letting go of her hand at last. “Hi. Good to meet you.” He turned slightly to one side, lowering his chin toward her shoulder and giving her just enough of a smile, again, to signal that they were done talking now—just as the people from the hallway stepped into the common room.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

segment:
He grinned some more, and let go. “Have you been here before?”
She hadn’t. But it was like the other Fulcrum facilities. There was the polished concrete floor, the wide open spaces with small clusters of furniture—that couch, a dining table, a coffee table—and an emphasis on sunlight and views of the outside world.

“No, not here.” She looked around at the common area and the huge windows that opened it up to the evening view. She recognized the furniture she had seen in the photos from her interview, but there was no one else yet. “I didn’t realize I would be early.”
He looked embarrassed. “Sorry. I just—” He hesitated for a moment before going on: “I just wanted to get out of the house. Get some fresh air and a good view.” His smile was more open and less apologetic now. “You can blame Livia.”

segment:
“Sorry,” Jonah said, and let go of her fingers. “I’m not one of those Fulcrum people who actually works here, so I’m not even allowed to know how to say hello to new people.” He grinned at his own joke, gesturing for her to walk around the room with him. “My name is Jonah Reed,” he said, “and I’m a hardware-security researcher in the private sector. I work on ways to hack into the chips and firmware on things that have been built, and ways to stop other people doing that. It’s not especially relevant to anything I’ve done at Fulcrum.”

“It sounds interesting,” Mara replied. She didn’t know what to say next. “I work in infrastructure security, too, but mine is all software-based. I haven’t learned that much about the hardware side of things.”
“Infrastructure,” Jonah repeated. “Is that like making sure that stuff doesn’t crash?”
“That, among other things,” Mara replied. The way he’d said it implied that she was missing his point, or that there was no point to be missed. She wasn’t sure.
